title: How I utilize body part splits for maximum muscle hypertrophy (versus upper lower
summary: A defense of body part splits for natural lifters, against their bad reputation online. He argues you should group muscles that work together around one compound lift (bench, squat, deadlift), then branch out into varied accessories where most of the volume and growth happens. Days should alternate upper and lower so heavily taxed muscles recover. He finds this better than upper/lower or push/pull/legs, because those structures handle deadlifts and leg frequency badly.

claims.claim: Body part splits have a bad reputation on YouTube and forums as worthless for naturals; he argues that done properly they are the best system for natural bodybuilders, for both size and strength.
He ran a body part split when he did powerlifting as a beginner and it worked for him.
A day of only triceps exercises isn't a real body part split: triceps are a small muscle that works together with the chest and shoulders.
Build split days around groups of muscles that work together, e.g. chest, shoulders and triceps on the same day.
Base each split day on a compound lift that trains the whole muscle group; the bench press covers chest, shoulders and triceps, which is why he says 'bench day', 'squat day', 'deadlift day'.
The anchor lift doesn't have to be one of the big three; any multi-joint compound that hits the same muscles works (e.g. weighted dips or weighted push-ups for chest).

A chest/shoulders/triceps day should open with bench and bench variations, then add accessories and isolation for muscles presses under-train: skull crushers for the triceps long head, overhead press, front and side raises, rear delt work.
Don't get stuck thinking only compound movements matter; even if bench is the best chest builder, it shouldn't be all you do.

Branch out across movement patterns instead of doing variations of a single lift (e.g. if your compound is weighted push-ups, add close-grip bench and overhead press rather than more push-up variants): it avoids injury, keeps you growing and keeps training fresh.
Doing the same movement again and again bores him to the point of not wanting to train.
The compound lift opens the session, but what follows it is what makes you grow, because that is where most of the volume is.
Arrange split days as upper, lower, upper, lower so the most heavily taxed muscles get time to recover.
With two squat days, make one hamstring-focused and the other quad-focused; a quad-heavy deadlift day must not follow a quad-focused squat day, or you won't recover and risk injury or stalled gains.
Body part splits are harder to program because everything must fit together, but once the puzzle fits it is one of the best systems you can run.
Upper/lower splits have no good place for deadlifts, which also train the upper back; adding pull-ups to a lower day makes it no longer a lower day.
Push/pull/legs works the legs on pull day too, and only trains legs once every three days; he wants to train legs and upper body about every 48 hours.
The body part split is the most flexible structure to tailor to individual needs and goals.
